A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same M-ABSA dataset and research work. Their main text, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: V1 reports original annotation agreement, translation-quality evaluations, mT5 and LLM experiments, and cross-lingual and cross-domain results.

after.justification: V2 retains these original empirical results and adds native-speaker evaluation of translation quality in Section 5.3 and Table 4.

M1.justification: The dataset construction, numbered aspect-marker translation, annotation projection and manual correction procedures are retained. The mT5 approach and LLM prompts are also unchanged; human evaluation adds validation rather than modifying the method.

E1.justification: Both versions cover the same seven domains, 21 languages, and TASD/UABSA tasks. Human evaluation samples existing translations. Cross-domain results for all languages already appeared across v1 Figure 5 and Appendix Figure 10.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison methods remain mT5-base, Llama-3.1 8B, Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 9B and Qwen-2.5 7B, alongside the random-pairing translation-quality baseline. The added related-work citation is not an evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a substantial human-evaluation protocol: 70 sentences per language, comprising ten per domain, for eight languages; three native speakers per language; and five dimensions rated from 1 to 5. Existing benchmark splits, micro-F1 evaluation, prompts and training settings are retained.

E4.justification: Section 5.3 and Appendix G add native-speaker validation of grammar, fluency, adequacy, code-switching and aspect-term translation, substantially extending the automatic translation-quality analyses in v1. Existing source-language, t-SNE and cross-domain analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over five random seeds and the same Sight annotation-agreement F1 scores. The new human study reports mean ratings without adding uncertainty estimates, significance tests or inter-rater agreement reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds human-evaluation results, including overall fluency of 3.61/5 and aspect-term translation of 4.27/5. Figure 3's English-source row is corrected from UABSA to existing TASD values, including English-to-Japanese 48.25 to 41.06. Table 3 gains averages and Table 1 loses token counts. Existing benchmark tables and cross-domain matrices otherwise retain their values.

T1.justification: The task definitions and mathematical content are retained. Neither version presents theoretical propositions or proofs; the new human-rating criteria introduce an empirical protocol rather than formal theory.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims about the multilingual parallel dataset, annotation-projection approach and evaluation applications. Human evaluation supplies additional support without redefining these core contributions.

C2.justification: V2 removes the Section 8 limitation identifying native-speaker evaluation as future work. Section 5.3 interprets the new ratings as supporting grammatical and semantic quality and aspect preservation. Other limitations and transfer explanations remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 documents human-evaluator recruitment, language qualifications, compensation, rating instructions and an interface example in Appendix G. Table 1 removes corpus token-count information. Existing model hyperparameters, software descriptions, prompts and code/data access information are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 adds Cai et al. (2025), MEMD-ABSA, and distinguishes its English-only coverage from multilingual resources. The remaining references and research positioning are substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 tightens passages in Sections 6.2–6.4, adds human-evaluation sections, rearranges appendix sections and updates author/affiliation text. The main narrative and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds the human-rating table and evaluation-interface figure, narrows Table 1 and adds Table 3's average row. English and Chinese cross-domain panels are consolidated with existing appendix panels in Figure 11. Other displays are largely retained and repositioned.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly identified missing native-speaker evaluation as a limitation. V2 addresses it across eight languages and all seven domains, providing substantial independent evidence about the central dataset-quality claim. Correcting Figure 3 also removes a task-mismatched comparison. These gains substantially strengthen validation, although the uniformly positive discussion underplays weaker ratings, such as Hindi aspect translation at 2.97/5 and Thai fluency at 2.81/5.
